n: In this lecture we will consider the organisation of forensic chemical examination. The plan is as follows: organisation of forensic chemical examination, expert chemists, rules for examination of physical evidence, examination documents and the report. Key expressions: forensic chemical examination, forensic chemists, expert chemists, the report and the documents of forensic chemical examination. First of all know this: forensic medical and forensic chemical examination is directed by the Chief Forensic Medical Expert at the Ministry of Health.

Forensic chemical examination has two aims. The first aim is to help judicial and investigating staff to clarify unclear questions on the basis of the knowledge of the science of forensic chemistry. The second aim is to help health workers prevent poisoning in industry, daily life and the national economy. That is, the examination serves investigation on the one hand and prevention on the other. The examination determines whether there is a poison harmful to human health or leading to death, and its quality and quantity.

Analysis is divided into two kinds. Directed analysis is carried out for one or several substances on the instruction of forensic medical or judicial and investigating staff. Undirected, or general, analysis is carried out for the 67 poisonous and potent substances included in the order of the Ministry of Health. This means that if the order does not specify which poison to test for, testing is carried out for the poisonous substances approved by the ministry. Remember the difference: in directed analysis the substance is specified, in general analysis testing is by list.

Now the legal basis. The organisation of forensic chemical examination rests on the judicial-procedural code and the People's Commissariat order of 4 July 1939. Among documents of great importance are No. 166 of 10 April 1962 and No. 694 of 21 June 1978. Also noted are the 1952 guide to organisation and the 1957 rules of the forensic chemical department. In the table the guide to organisation is shown with the date 13 December 1952. These are historical documents showing the basis of the organisation of the examination.

We move to the current regulatory basis. The Law “On Forensic Examination” was approved by the Legislative Chamber on 18 November 2009 and by the Senate on 7 May 2010; the law came into force on 1 June 2010. There are also orders of the Ministry of Health: of 25 July 2011, No. 153 of 1 July 2012 and No. 82 of 15 April 2015. According to Presidential Resolution No. PQ-4049 of 4 December 2018, the Main Bureau was transformed into the Republican Scientific and Practical Centre of Forensic Medical Examination, that is, the Centre. The bureaux of the regions and the city of Tashkent were reorganised as branches of the Centre.

The procedure of directing the examination is as follows. Forensic medical and forensic chemical examination is directed by the Chief Forensic Medical Expert at the ministry. In managerial work he is subordinate to the ministry or its first deputy. In scientific and practical work, however, he is subordinate to the forensic medical research institute. Look at the chain in the diagram: Ministry of Health, Chief Forensic Medical Expert, Republican Centre, and then regional and city branches.

In the structure of the Republican Centre the director has three deputies. The deputy for scientific work is responsible for the scientific department, laboratory investigations and information and communication technology. The deputy for expert work directs organisational-methodological and quality control, complex examination and the medico-criminalistic directions. The deputy for general matters heads the finance-accounting department, personnel, legal service, chancellery and economic department. Thus scientific, expert and general work are separated.

Now the departments of the Centre. They are as follows: the organisational-methodological department and quality control department, and also the department of complex examinations. Then there is the medico-criminalistic department, within which the spectral and radiological units work. The forensic biological department stands together with the unit for molecular-genetic investigation of DNA. Most important for us: the forensic chemical department with its biochemical investigation unit, and also the forensic histology department, belong to the Centre.

t: Rooms of the forensic chemical department
n: The department in which forensic chemical examination is carried out must have at least 5 rooms. In the diagram the rooms are shown in order: the first is the reception and storage room, with a refrigerator and an iron safe. The second is the laboratory, where investigation and examination are carried out. The third is the sample preparation room, in which the external appearance of the physical evidence is studied. The fourth is working rooms, that is, offices. The fifth is the room where reagents and other materials are kept. The number of rooms and the staff instructions are given in the “Rules” approved by the Chief Forensic Medical Expert.

The laboratory regime is strict. All rooms of the laboratory are locked after work and sealed with lead. There must be a separate cold room for physical evidence and a separate room for poisonous substances. In the forensic chemical department there are three posts: senior chemist, who is regarded as head of department, then chemist and laboratory assistant. Remember: physical evidence and poisonous substances are not kept in one room; a separate room is allotted to each.

The duties of the forensic chemist are divided into four directions. First, to conduct forensic chemical examination on the basis of an order of the judicial and investigating bodies, in some cases at the request of forensic medical experts and medical institutions. Second, on the summons of investigating bodies, to attend under any conditions in order to answer questions. Third, on completion of the examination, to record the outcome of the analysis, which is called the report. Fourth, the chemist must have higher education in the pharmacist specialty, complete the specialty course and take a refresher course every 5 years.

This slide gives the chemist's duties according to the qualification material, year 2012. The first duty: to receive the physical evidence and documents attached to it from the head of the forensic medical laboratory. Second: in the forensic chemical laboratory, to check the list of examinations and carry out analyses. Third: to record in the work notebook the methods of investigation, their course and results. Fourth: to write forensic chemical reports and consult judicial institutions on important information.

The expert chemist has four rights. The first is to become acquainted with the case materials. The second is to demand additional materials. The third is to be present at judicial and investigating sessions in the case. And finally, the rights of experts are equated with those of forensic medical experts. This means that the expert chemist stands at the same level legally as the forensic medical expert. At the same time, the rights to become acquainted with case materials, to demand additional materials and to be present at judicial and investigating sessions are listed separately.

t: Expert chemist: duties and rights compared
n: Now we compare duties and rights side by side. Duties: to carry out the examination on the basis of the order, to attend on summons, to write the report after the examination and to take a refresher every 5 years. Rights: to become acquainted with case materials, to demand additional materials and to be present at judicial and investigating sessions. The rights of experts are equated with those of forensic medical experts. That is, a duty is work that the chemist must perform, whereas a right is an opportunity granted to him or her.

t: Expert's rights: text of the Law
n: This slide gives the expert's rights according to the text of the Law. The expert becomes acquainted with the case materials, takes copies of them and petitions for additional materials and objects to be provided. At investigative actions he or she is present with the permission of the inquirer, investigator or prosecutor; at court hearings, with the court's permission, he or she asks questions. If he or she does not know the language of the proceedings, he or she presents the conclusion in the native language and uses the services of an interpreter. If rights are violated, he or she appeals against decisions and actions in the manner established by law.

t: Expert's obligations: text of the Law
n: Now the expert's obligations, which are also based on the text of the Law. The expert examines the objects provided thoroughly and fully and gives a reasoned and impartial conclusion on the questions. On the summons of the inquiry, investigation or court, he or she appears in person and answers additional questions to explain the conclusion. He or she does not disclose information that has become known in connection with the examination; ensures the preservation of objects and case materials. He or she has no right to report the result to anyone other than the body, that is, the person, that ordered the examination, or to collect materials independently.

On ethics and deontology. Deontology is from the Greek deon, that is, what is necessary, and logos, that is, I study. It is the knowledge that studies the aim and laws of full clarification of the case. The ethics and deontology of the forensic chemist are equal to, and directly linked with, the norms of law and justice. Therefore every expert chemist must observe the necessary ethics and deontology in his or her activity.

Ethical requirements lie in several directions. In conversation with the victim or relatives, the expert does not raise his or her voice and does not ask questions that touch pride or are inappropriate. Straightforwardness, truthfulness and honesty are required of the expert; an extremely sensitive and gentle attitude to close relatives is necessary. Keeping the causes of the incident confidential is the professional duty of forensic medical and forensic chemical experts. Remember: experts who disclose examination data are brought to administrative liability.

We become acquainted with the procedure for sending physical evidence for examination. The protocol of the order, an extract from the forensic medical report and, if the person was in hospital, from the case history are sent. Physical evidence and documents are entered in the laboratory's registration journal. The chain is as follows: order for examination, office, that is, chancellery, registration journal, handing over to the forensic chemist, and examination according to plan. If the packaging has been broken, the examination is carried out after a report has been drawn up.

t: Order for examination and the expert's responsibility
n: The order for examination must state the circumstances of the crime, the physical evidence and the task set for the forensic chemist. The expert chemist is responsible for preserving the physical evidence received from the start to the end of the examination. Bear in mind that this is his or her personal responsibility. In addition, with the aim of providing urgent medical help, examination may also be carried out on the instruction of judicial and investigating bodies or on the written instruction of a hospital. That is, the circumstances of the crime, the physical evidence and the task stated in the order determine the direction of the chemist's work.

t: The order and the set of documents sent
n: We consider the set of documents sent. The order for the examination must state the commission of the crime, the physical evidence and the task set before the forensic chemist. To the laboratory are sent the written protocol of the order and an extract from the forensic medical report. If the deceased lay in hospital, an extract from the case history is also sent. That is, the set consists of three parts: the protocol of the order, the extract from the forensic medical report and the case history.

At the reception stage, physical evidence must be packed and sealed by the body that ordered the examination, and listed in the attached documents. The expert chemist describes the type of packaging, the condition of the seal, the dimensions and the inscriptions. The packaging is opened carefully: the container must not be damaged and the object must not be lost. Documents are kept in a separate folder in a safe or metal cabinet. These rules are taken from the draft rules. Thus when physical evidence is received, its packaging, seal and inscriptions are described first, and only after that is it opened.

t: On opening the packaging: discrepancy and contamination
n: On opening the packaging, the question of discrepancy and contamination may arise. After the physical evidence is opened, the object in the jars is compared with the documents and its weight determined. If the object differs from that stated in the document, a commission of three people draws up a report; one copy is sent to the institution that sent it. There is a further risk: if fragments of the lead seal fall into the object, heavy metals may be detected in chemical examination.

The examination documents consist of three journals. In forensic chemical laboratories 3 journals are mainly kept. The first is the registration journal, which consists of 16 sections. The second is the forensic chemist's work notebook, in which daily calculations are recorded. The third is the report book; like the work notebook it is numbered, corded and sealed, and handwritten. The purpose of all three documents is different: one registers, one records calculations, and the third collects reports.

The rules for keeping the journals, according to the qualification material, are as follows. The pages of the registration journal are numbered, stitched with thread and sealed with lead. In the work notebook all of the chemist's chemical investigations and the external appearance of the object are recorded; the bureau seal is stamped on the notebook. The report journal is likewise numbered, stitched, sealed and signed by the head of the bureau. That is, each journal is drawn up in such a way that it cannot be corrected or replaced.

t: Data entered in the registration journal
n: A number of data are entered in the registration journal. They are: the serial number of receipt of the examination, the date of arrival, the number and date of the main attached document, and the number of sheets. Then the institution that sent the physical evidence, the person, that is, the surname of the deceased, the type of physical evidence and the number of objects. After that a brief description of the case, the purpose of the investigation, the surname of the expert chemist, and the start and end dates. Finally a brief statement of the result, the conclusion, that is, the report number, and a receipt of handover are written.

The last stage of the investigation is writing the report on the investigation of the physical evidence, or the expert conclusion. The report is drawn up after thorough study of the results of the investigation, on the basis of the entries made in the work notebook. The report consists of 4 parts: the introductory part, the appearance of the physical evidence, the chemical investigation and the expert's conclusion. Remember the order in the diagram. First the introductory part is written, then the appearance of the physical evidence, after that the chemical investigation is described, and the report is completed with the expert's conclusion. Each part has its own content.

In the introductory part of the report are stated on the basis of what document and in which laboratory the investigation was carried out, the full name of the expert, his or her post, degree and work notebook. Also written are the full name of the victim, the physical evidence sent, and the times the investigation began and finished. Information is also given about which poisonous substances must be tested for, the circumstances in which the crime was committed, and the documents sent with the physical evidence. This part establishes by whom, where and on what basis the investigation was carried out.

t: Four parts of the report: what is written
n: We summarise what is written in the four parts of the report. Part one, introductory: laboratory, full name and post of the expert, victim, physical evidence sent, time of investigation, which poison is tested for. Part two, appearance: packaging, container, sealing, colour, odour, weight, pH of the medium. Part three, chemical investigation: methods, reactions, reagents, calculations; writing formulae and citing the name of an author are prohibited. Part four, conclusion: first the substances found in mg / 100 g, then substances with a negative result.

On the part of the report devoted to appearance. In the description are written the full external appearance of the physical evidence, its packaging, container, sealing and the inscriptions on the packaging. The colour, odour, weight and pH of the medium of the physical evidence must be written. The agent used for preservation and the reaction to indicator papers are also noted. That is, every sign encountered in the external familiarisation with the object is entered in the report.

t: Chemical investigation part of the report
n: The chemical investigation part of the report is regarded as the main part. In it, methods, reactions, reagents and apparatus, and quantitative calculations are written in order on the basis of the work notebook. In this part of the report it is prohibited to write chemical formulae or to cite the name of any author. The expressions “the result of the reaction is positive or negative” are not used; the name of a substance is not written as a conclusion from a reaction. The quantitative method and calculation must be written so that, by repeating the analysis, the same result can be reached.

In the conclusion part of the report, the poisonous substances found are stated first; the amount is calculated in mg per 100 g of physical evidence. Then the poisonous substances fully investigated chemically and giving a negative result are stated. When ethyl alcohol is determined in blood and urine, the report is printed in two copies, sealed by the expert chemist, and the time of writing is stated. The seal of forensic medical examination is stamped on the report; one copy is handed to the relevant organisation, the second to the archive of forensic medical examination.

The requirements for writing the report, according to the qualification material, are as follows. The report is written separately for each object and by hand only; the use of ready-made forms is not permitted. No corrections are allowed in the report; if a correction is made, this is specially noted and confirmed by the signature of the forensic chemist. The product of a reaction, for example Prussian blue or the red precipitate of mercury(II) iodide, or a photograph of a crystal may be attached as physical evidence. The report is signed by the chemist; the second copy is handed to the judicial institution that sent it for examination.

t: Retention of physical evidence and documents
n: The retention periods for physical evidence and documents are of three kinds. A preserved object is kept for up to 1 year. Documents are kept in a safe and discarded after 1 year. Objects containing alcohol are discarded after 1 month. Distinguish the periods: 1 year for the preserved object and documents, 1 month for an object containing alcohol. The table also gives these three values: preserved object up to 1 year, documents in the safe 1 year, object containing alcohol 1 month.

t: Circumstances taken into account in assessing results
n: In assessing results, several reasons for a substance not being found are taken into account. The substance may have been eliminated from the body before death or have undergone metabolic change. The substance may break down altogether or combine with other substances. One more reason: the substance may not be determined because the sensitivity of the method is low. Remember: quantitative analysis is always carried out for a substance that has been determined.

t: A substance found is not always a poison
n: A substance found is not always a poison. First, the victim may have taken the substance as a medicine. Second, the substance found may be natural to the object, for example metals. Third, as a result of putrefaction of the object, compounds may form that give reactions characteristic of the substance being sought. Fourth, some substance from the external environment may have been added to the object; reactions characteristic of a harmless substance may also appear. Therefore caution is necessary in assessing the result.

We conclude the topic. The examination serves two aims: assistance to judicial and investigating bodies and prevention of poisoning. Documents: 3 journals and a report of 4 parts; retention periods: 1 year, 1 year and 1 month. In assessing the result, elimination, metabolism, breakdown, combination and the sensitivity of the method are taken into account. Review questions: the rooms of the forensic chemical department, the rights and obligations of the expert, the parts of the report.

t: Report on ethyl alcohol: route of copies
n: When ethyl alcohol is determined in blood and urine, the forensic chemical report is printed in two copies. The expert chemist seals the report and states the time of writing, and then the seal of forensic medical examination is stamped. One copy, with the serial number stated, is sent to the relevant organisation, and the second is kept in the archive of forensic medical examination. The route in the diagram is this: the report is printed in 2 copies, the expert seals it and writes the time, the seal of forensic medical examination is stamped, copy 1 goes to the organisation, copy 2 to the archive.
